material_units.source_text: No previous probability course is needed. Start with events and finite probability tables, then conditioning and transitions. Gaussian formulas use the matrix review in Primer A; the probability language is introduced here. Treat the measure-theory background and longer proofs as a second pass after you can do the Easy and Medium problems.
material_units.per_unit_reason: This paragraph recommends a study order and prerequisites, including an optional second pass through background proofs; it contains no probability formula or theorem.

material_units.source_text: Begin with the three readiness checks. If a check is difficult, use its review link and worked answer, then try again without looking. After each section, try its Easy problem, use the separate hint if needed, and continue to Medium once you can explain the steps. Hard problems combine ideas or expose a common mistake. Keep the answers closed on your first attempt.
material_units.per_unit_reason: The paragraph instructs the learner to attempt readiness checks, use hints and progress by difficulty; its explanation of problem categories is pedagogical.

material_units.source_text: No previous RL or neural-network course is needed. First trace one state–action–reward–next-state transition, then compute a short discounted return. Sections 1–4 explain what is being solved; sections 5–6 explain learning methods. Sections 7–9 form a second strand about the networks used as policies or models. You can begin that strand after refreshing matrix multiplication and the chain rule, even while the policy-gradient material is still new.
material_units.per_unit_reason: The paragraph recommends tracing a transition, computing a return and following the numbered instructional strands; it states no return formula or algorithmic guarantee.
